newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Gloom starts to lift for South African markets.
newsitem.headline: Gloom starts to lift for South African markets.

text.p: Seven months after the first rand meltdown, shaky South African markets may be finding their feet, helped by a modest cut in interest rates and a successful 1996 wage round, analysts said on Thursday.
The country's big banks on Thursday fell into line with the lead set by Standard Bank, cutting their prime overdraft rates by a 0.25 point to 19.25 percent from October 1.
The reduction helped the bond market to its best levels in nearly two months with the yield on the key R150 stock nearing 15 percent, 75 basis points down from the beginning of August.
A further boost to sentiment came from successful deals struck by the 350,000-strong National Union of Mineworkers.
On Wednesday, the union clinched an accord for gold and coal miners, and on Thursday struck agreement with diamond giant De Beers -- in both cases averting damaging strikes.
Coupled with three weeks' relative stability in the rand and signs the currency's fall is feeding through into an improved balance of payments, optimists believe the tide is on the turn.
"I think there's a change in sentiment and as soon as that happens all markets will start to look at fundamentals again," said SMK Securities economist Herman van Papendorp.
"The fundamentals of the South African economy, in terms of low inflation and so on, look very good. When the market turns around, the correction could be quite substantial."

Peter Worthington, emerging market analyst at J.P. Morgan in London, also detects a change of mood with a steadier rand since mid-August tempting back investors who have been scared off by the currency risk of South Africa this year.
"I think that the rand has really plateaued for a while...My sense is that there may be a shift in sentiment," he said.

The rand this week fell back below the pyschologically-significant level of 7.0 against sterling and has also held its own against a strong dollar. It last traded at 4.49 against the U.S. currency, 10 cents up on its record low set in August, though a far cry from the 3.65 it was worth throughout most of 1995.

Analysts said this week's strike-free wage deals helped counter South Africa's poor labour reputation, while wage rises of eight to 10 percent were moderate given inflation was likely to reach this level by year-end from July's 7.1 percent.

In the medium term, however, the government still needed to deliver evidence of its success in implementing its macro-economic strategy, unveiled in June and designed to double growth to six percent a year by 2000.
"People will need to watch next year's budget (in March) very carefully because that is the one that will actually put flesh on the macro-economic strategy," Worthington said.

Rudolf Gouws, chief economist at Rand Merchant Bank, said South Africa was now emerging from its financial crisis with the balance of payments likely to improve dramatically, boosting official reserves which slipped to just one month's import cover in August.
That view was echoed by Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals who on Wednesday told investors in Zurich the country's current account deficit would begin to shrink in line with an economic slowdown.
The first signs of the turnaround came with a surprise surge in the trade surplus in August.

Officials predict the economy will expand by some three percent in 1996, on the surface little changed from 1995's 3.3 percent. But this year's increase is deceptive since the main impetus comes from a jump in agricultural production.
Gouws predicts the slowdown will allow for a gradual easing in interest rates over the next 18 months with the short-end likely to shed some 300 basis points and the long end 150-200 basis points.
